title: Brazil’s 2026 Election: What to Know and What’s at Stake | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Brazil's October 4, 2026 general election is effectively a Lula vs. Flávio Bolsonaro rematch of 2022 by proxy, fought over security, corruption, affordability and sovereignty amid U.S. tariffs. A Bolsonaro win would tilt Brazil toward Washington, the Shield of the Americas and away from BRICS, though experts expect either winner to keep economically necessary ties with both the U.S. and China.

themes.theme: Race structure: Lula vs. Flávio Bolsonaro

insights.claim: Of thirteen candidates in Brazil's October 4, 2026 presidential election, only incumbent Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro consistently poll in double digits; a runoff is held October 25 if no one exceeds 50 percent.
insights.speaker: Mary Kate Godfrey
insights.so_what: A two-horse race with a likely runoff extends political uncertainty for Brazilian assets through late October.

insights.claim: FGV professor Oliver Stuenkel argues Brazil's weak party system rewards personalistic leadership, making the election a proxy rematch of 2022 in which voters decide for or against Lula and the Bolsonaro family, driven more by fear of the other side than by policy.
insights.speaker: Mary Kate Godfrey
insights.so_what: Negative-partisanship-driven outcomes are harder to forecast from policy platforms; polarization likely persists post-election regardless of winner.

insights.claim: The 80-year-old Lula seeks a historic fourth term on a platform of reducing inequality, expanding industry, promoting sustainability, defending sovereignty against foreign interference and broadening geopolitical partnerships, after modest economic improvements in his third term.
insights.speaker: Mary Kate Godfrey
insights.so_what: A Lula win implies policy continuity: industrial policy, fiscal looseness concerns and multi-aligned diplomacy.

insights.speaker: Mary Kate Godfrey
insights.so_what: An amnesty push would reopen institutional conflict with the judiciary, a governance-risk factor if Bolsonaro wins.

themes.theme: Security and crime as top voter issue

insights.claim: In a September Quaest/Pax survey, 28 percent of Brazilians named violence as the country's main problem, ahead of corruption and the economy.
insights.speaker: Mary Kate Godfrey
insights.so_what: Security is the decisive campaign issue, favoring hard-line platforms.

insights.claim: Criminal groups are expanding territory and infiltrating Brazil's political and judicial system; in December 2025 the head of Rio de Janeiro's state assembly was arrested for alleged links to Red Command.
insights.speaker: Mary Kate Godfrey
insights.so_what: Organized-crime penetration of institutions is a structural governance risk for investors in Brazil.

insights.claim: Bolsonaro's twelve-point security plan would designate criminal groups as narcoterrorist organizations and build El Salvador-style maximum-security prisons, but Stuenkel says such measures intuitively appeal to voters yet are unlikely to meaningfully reduce insecurity.

insights.so_what: Narcoterrorist designations could align Brazil with U.S. counter-cartel framing, but expect limited actual security improvement.

insights.claim: Per a September Quaest survey, 33 percent of Brazilians say their income did not rise in the past year and 21 percent say it rose but failed to keep pace with living costs, despite a falling poverty rate since 2022.

insights.so_what: Cost-of-living discontent undercuts the incumbent's economic record and pressures any winner toward populist spending.

insights.claim: Experts expect either winner to maintain ties with both the U.S. and China out of economic necessity, since they are Brazil's top two trading partners and main markets for beef, soybeans and iron ore, and China is a growing investor in Brazilian critical-minerals mining.
